title: Borrowed Youth, Disposable Flesh, and the Runaway Engine: Antagonistic Pleiotropy, Disposable Soma Theory & the mTOR Hyperfunction Challenge — The immortal germline vs. aging paradox; Williams's 1957 nine predictions & Kirkwood's 1977 somatic error-budget optimization; Rodríguez's 2017 human GWAS scan & Long and Zhang's 2019 leukemia-outlier audit paving the way for 276,406 UK Biobank genomes; Jones's 46-species desert-tortoise & Hydra negative senescence, Clancy's shifted chico dietary-restriction peaks & Blagosklonny and Gems's mTOR geroconversion hyperfunction; Hamilton selection-shadow & Kirkwood repair-allocation math, 2x2 Schoenfeld survival interaction power & spotting aging theories in disguise

teenKit.tldr: Your body doesn't age because it simply wears out like an old car; instead, evolution trades your long-term maintenance for early survival and reproduction.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding that aging is driven by overactive biological growth pathways rather than passive decay transforms how we approach treating age-related diseases and extending health.
keyTakeaways: Natural selection is obsessed with passing on genes early in life, even if it sets a ticking time bomb for your body decades later.
The Disposable Soma Theory proves that energy spent repairing cells is energy stolen from making babies, forcing the body to balance a strict metabolic budget.
The mTOR Hyperfunction Theory suggests aging is not a lack of maintenance, but rather a developmental engine stuck at full throttle that drugs like rapamycin can potentially brake.

vocab.meaning: When a single gene helps you thrive and reproduce when you are young, but actively destroys your health when you get older.
The idea that evolution treats your body like a disposable vehicle, investing just enough energy to keep it running until reproduction is done before cutting maintenance funds.
A biological growth pathway that refuses to turn off once you reach adulthood, causing cellular damage through developmental run-on.
A rare biological cheat code where an organism's risk of dying actually decreases as it gets older, seen in creatures like Hydra and desert tortoises.

quiz.question: According to George C. Williams's Antagonistic Pleiotropy, why does natural selection allow our bodies to fall apart after age thirty?
options: Because our DNA completely stops replicating once we reach adulthood.
Because genes that boost early survival and reproduction are favored, even if they carry deadly side effects later in life.
Because older humans consume too many planetary resources, triggering a genetic kill-switch.
Because the sun's radiation slowly destroys our cells faster than they can divide.
quiz.explanation: Evolution prioritizes genes that help you win the evolutionary game early on, trading away your long-term maintenance.

quiz.question: What is the core argument of Thomas Kirkwood's Disposable Soma Theory?
options: Organisms have a limited metabolic budget and must choose between investing in reproduction or cellular repair.
The body's cells are completely replaced every seven years, leading to copying errors.
Somatic cells are immortal if kept in a nutrient-rich laboratory environment.
Aging is caused exclusively by toxic waste buildup in the bloodstream.
quiz.explanation: Energy spent fixing damaged somatic cells cannot be used to make babies, forcing a strict evolutionary compromise.

quiz.question: How does the mTOR Hyperfunction Theory fundamentally challenge traditional views of aging?
options: It proves that aging is a passive, inevitable wearing-out of mechanical parts like an old engine.
It claims that aging is caused by a lack of calories and can be cured by eating more sugar.
It argues that aging is driven by a developmental growth program that stays jammed at full throttle instead of passively decaying.
It states that humans age because our germline cells finally run out of divisions.
quiz.explanation: Instead of passive wear-and-tear, mTOR hyperfunction views aging as a hyper-active biological run-on that keeps pushing growth when it should be braking.
